passages.t: ‘My heart is steadfast, O God’: two old psalms joined
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A song. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The psalm begins in confidence. “My heart is steadfast, O God; I will sing and make music with all my being” (verse 1). The singer will wake his harp and lyre, and then wake the dawn itself (verse 2). He will praise God among the nations (verse 3), “For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens” (verse 4).

Then he prays. “Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered” (verse 6). God answers from his sanctuary and claims the land as his own, piece by piece: Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim and Judah (verses 7 and 8). The neighbouring peoples are given humble places: “Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal” (verse 9).

The psalm ends with a hard question and a firm hope. “Have You not rejected us, O God?” (verse 11). “Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless” (verse 12). “With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
If these lines sound familiar, they are. Verses 1 to 5 are almost the same as Psalm 57:7-11. Verses 6 to 13 are almost the same as Psalm 60:5-12. Read the notes on Psalms 57 and 60 for what those lines meant first.

Psalm 57 was a prayer from a cave while David hid from Saul. Psalm 60 was a prayer after a defeat in battle. Psalm 108 leaves out both of their dark openings. It begins with the confident ending of 57 and moves straight into the promise of 60. Someone shaped old words for a new need. When that was done is not known. Many scholars think it was done after the exile; others think it could be earlier.

Israel treated its songs as living things. Psalms 14 and 53 are nearly the same, and Psalm 70 repeats the end of Psalm 40. Using old prayers again in a new day is not a lack of new ideas. It is how a people keeps praying.

The pictures in verse 9 are pictures of rank. A washbasin was a lowly household bowl. Tossing a sandal may be a sign of scorn, or a sign of taking ownership. In Ruth, a man gave his sandal to make a land deal binding (Ruth 4:7). Readers take it both ways.
passages.later:
Judah as God's ‘scepter’ (verse 8) recalls Jacob's blessing: “The scepter will not depart from Judah” (Genesis 49:10).

‘The help of man is worthless’ is a thread through Book Five. Psalm 118 says, “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man” (Psalm 118:8). Paul asks the same question with the same trust: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).
passages.asks:
The singer says his heart is ‘steadfast’, that is, fixed and settled. In Psalm 57 he said this from inside a cave. Steadiness in God is not the same as calm circumstances.

You may also borrow old prayers for your own day. Psalm 108 shows that God's people have always done it. A prayer you learned long ago may be exactly the prayer you need now.
